summaries.example: Imagine two sentence cards: “The light is on” and “The door is open.” The word “and” joins them. In formal logic, a connective such as ∧ is a carefully studied version of “and.” A valuation gives each sentence either True or False. For ∧, the result is True only when both cards are True. Logicians also study whether rules for a connective really control its behavior, and whether two different connectives can have the same logical effects.
summaries.summary: Formal logic uses connectives to build sentences and studies their rules and patterns. Examples include conjunction, disjunction, implication, and negation. A valuation labels formulas True or False. A truth-functional connective gets its result entirely from the labels of its parts. The entry also studies sequents, which display assumptions and conclusions, and rules that transform one sequent into another. A central theme is that properties depend on the logic and proof system being used. A connective may preserve equivalence inside larger sentences, or it may fail to do so. The article examines whether rules are enough to make a connective exist, whether they uniquely identify it, and whether adding a proposed connective leaves the old logic unchanged. Strange proposed connectives show why careful rules matter: a rule set can accidentally make every statement follow from every other statement. The discussion also compares ordinary one-conclusion logic with multiple-conclusion logic, where a set of possible conclusions is allowed. This broader framework can describe some truth-function behavior that the narrower framework cannot enforce directly.
key_ideas: Formal logic studies the behavior of sentence connectives, not mainly the everyday meanings of words such as “and” or “if.”
Truth-functionality means that the truth value of a compound is fixed by the truth values of its parts.
Different proof systems can give different rules for the same-looking connective.
A logic may use one-sided conclusions or conclusions written as a set; this choice can affect which connectives are fully described.
The entry asks whether connectives with certain rules exist, whether they are unique, and whether adding them changes old arguments.
summaries.why_it_matters: Connectives appear in mathematics, computer science, and careful everyday reasoning. Knowing how their rules work helps us tell a valid argument from an invalid one. The entry also teaches an important lesson about definitions: adding a new symbol is not harmless unless its rules fit with the old system. Studying different proof systems shows why the design of a logic can change what its symbols mean and what they can express.

important_terms.definition: A symbol or operation used to build a larger sentence from one or more smaller sentences, such as “and,” “or,” or “not.”
A way of assigning True or False to every formula in a formal language.
A function whose output depends only on the True-or-False inputs it receives.
A statement that says what follows from some starting statements.
A formal rule for moving from one sequent, or argument pattern, to another.

questions_to_think_about: Why might the word “or” be harder to model exactly than the word “and”?
Can two different sets of rules describe the same connective?
What should happen if a new connective lets us prove an old statement that was not provable before?

summaries.example: Consider two Boolean valuations u and v. Let u make p true and q false, while v makes p false and q true. Their conjunctive combination can be understood as keeping only what both valuations make true. It makes p and q false, yet it still makes p ∨ q true, because both original valuations made that disjunction true. If ∨ had any single truth-function on this combined valuation, that function would have to send (False, False) to True. But p ∨ p would then be True, even though p is False; this conflicts with the classical consequence p ∨ p ⊢ p. The example shows that a connective can fail even to be pseudo-truth-functional on a class of valuations consistent with a consequence relation.
summaries.summary: The entry investigates formal representatives of natural-language connectives, leaving aside the separate questions of which expressions are logical constants and whether formal rules capture ordinary meaning. It treats languages algebraically, with connectives as operations, and studies consequence relations, valuations, sequents, and sequent-to-sequent rules. A valuation assigns True or False to formulas. Truth-functionality requires a single truth-function to govern a connective throughout a class of valuations; pseudo-truth-functionality permits different functions on different members. These notions are relative to a chosen class of valuations and, indirectly, to a logic or framework. The distinction between Set–Fmla sequents and Set–Set sequents is central. Ordinary consequence relations have closure features that can prevent them from excluding certain unwanted valuations, while generalized consequence relations can state determinant-by-determinant conditions more directly. Nevertheless, ordinary consequence relations can still distinguish any two distinct truth-functions of the same arity. The entry connects semantic properties with proof-theoretic ones. Full determination corresponds, in suitable settings, to truth-functionality; extensionality corresponds to pseudo-truth-functionality; congruentiality is weaker still. It then studies whether rule sets define connectives, whether those connectives are unique, and whether adding them is conservative. The Tonk example shows that rules resembling familiar introduction and elimination rules may yield triviality. Id-inductivity is linked with uniqueness, while Cut-inductivity is linked with conservative-extension behavior, although the relationships are not simple equivalences. key_ideas: The article distinguishes the connective as a syntactic operation from a connective understood through its inferential behavior in a particular logic.
Truth-functionality has an existential-universal structure: one truth-function must work for every valuation in the chosen class. Pseudo-truth-functionality allows the function to vary by valuation.

Ordinary consequence relations are less expressive than generalized, or multiple-conclusion, consequence relations in some respects; for example, they are closed under conjunctive combinations of valuations.
Full determination, extensionality, and congruentiality form a hierarchy of increasingly weaker properties, though the reverse implications generally fail.
Rules can be sound and complete for a valuation class without forcing every valuation consistent with the resulting consequence relation to interpret the connective in the intended way.
The Tonk-style case illustrates nonconservativity: individually plausible introduction and elimination rules can combine to derive arbitrary old-language sequents.
summaries.why_it_matters: The analysis matters because formal logic is not merely a list of symbols. A connective receives its role through syntax, semantics, rules, and the framework in which those rules operate. This helps explain why classical and intuitionistic logic can treat familiar connectives differently, why a proof system may underdetermine a semantic interpretation, and why apparently innocent extensions can destroy conservativity. These issues are relevant to automated reasoning, programming-language design, algebraic logic, and philosophical accounts of logical meaning.

important_terms.definition: A formula formed from propositional variables by applying primitive operations of specified numbers of inputs, or arities.
A function from truth values of n inputs to a truth value; a connective is truth-functional when one such function governs it across a class of valuations.
A relation between sets of premises and a conclusion, recording when the conclusion follows according to a logic.
An ordered display of premises and one or more conclusions, often written with a sequent arrow between them.
The property that equivalent formulas remain interchangeable when placed inside every relevant context, according to a logic.
An extension that adds symbols or rules without producing new consequences stated entirely in the old language.
The relation in which every principle holding for one connective also holds for another, in the relevant logical framework.
A proof-theoretic property in which rules for a connective support identity and cut behavior in the corresponding sequent calculus.

questions_to_think_about: Why does allowing several conclusions change which truth-functions can be characterized directly by sequents?
Should a connective count as meaningful if its rules are conservative but do not preserve old synonymies?
What is lost when a logic is identified only with its consequence relation rather than with a particular proof system?
Can a connective be uniquely characterized without being fully truth-functional?

summaries.example: Suppose a game uses the statement “Maya brought juice or fruit.” In ordinary conversation, “or” can suggest different things depending on context. Formal logic sets that conversational issue aside and asks how a symbol ∨ behaves according to rules or truth assignments. In classical logic, ∨ is true when at least one input is true. But a proof system may have trouble forcing every compatible valuation to use exactly that truth table. A broader sequent system, which can list several possible conclusions, can state more of the needed information directly. This is one reason logicians compare different kinds of sequents instead of assuming that one format is best for every purpose.
summaries.summary: Sentence connectives are formal operations modeled on expressions such as “and,” “or,” “if,” and “not.” The entry does not settle which natural-language expressions should count as logical constants or whether formal logic captures every aspect of their ordinary meanings. Instead, it studies the formal representatives themselves. Formal languages contain formulas built from sentence letters and primitive connectives. A valuation assigns truth values to formulas, and a truth-function specifies an output truth value for every possible pattern of inputs. A connective is truth-functional relative to a class of valuations when one function works for all of them; it is pseudo-truth-functional when an appropriate function may differ from one valuation to another. The article emphasizes that these properties depend on the chosen logic and proof system. It introduces consequence relations, sequents, and rules. In a one-conclusion framework, premises lead to one formula. In a multiple-conclusion framework, the right side may contain a set of formulas, representing alternatives in a way that can express more semantic constraints. The entry compares semantic descriptions with proof-theoretic descriptions. It asks whether rules are enough to establish a connective’s existence, whether they uniquely characterize it, and whether adding the rules is conservative. The famous Tonk-style pattern illustrates a warning: combining an introduction rule modeled on disjunction with an elimination rule modeled on conjunction can make arbitrary conclusions derivable. Other topics include congruentiality, extensionality, hybrids of connectives, subconnectives, and questions about connectives that mimic or modify familiar truth-functions.
key_ideas: The entry studies formal connectives and their relations, rather than deciding the everyday meanings of words such as “if” or “or.”
A connective is truth-functional when one truth table works throughout a chosen class of valuations; pseudo-truth-functionality is a weaker, valuation-by-valuation version.
Whether a connective has a property is often relative to a logic, a proof system, or a class of valuations.
Sequents can have one conclusion or several conclusions. This framework choice affects what can be expressed and which valuations can be ruled out.
Rules for a connective may be sound and useful without completely fixing its intended interpretation.
Existence and uniqueness questions ask whether a connective with certain behavior can be added safely and whether another connective governed by the same rules would behave equivalently.
summaries.why_it_matters: These questions show why logical notation cannot be understood by appearance alone. Two symbols may look similar while having different rules, and one set of rules may behave differently in different proof frameworks. Careful study of connectives helps philosophers compare classical and intuitionistic reasoning and helps logicians design systems that remain consistent, informative, and conservative when new expressive tools are added.

important_terms.definition: A logical symbol that combines one or more formulas, including symbols modeled on “and,” “or,” “if,” and “not.”
An assignment of True or False to formulas, subject to whatever behavior the chosen connectives are required to have.
A rule-like function that determines an output truth value from input truth values.
A relation saying that a conclusion follows from a group of premises in a particular logic.
A formal arrangement of premises and a conclusion, or premises and a set of conclusions.
A property of a logic in which equivalent formulas can be substituted within larger formulas without changing their equivalence.
An addition to a logical system that does not create new results using only the original vocabulary.
A connective whose logical principles are included among those of another connective in a specified setting.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a formal symbol need rules as well as a truth table?
How could adding a new connective accidentally change arguments that never mention it?
Why might two connectives share some logical principles without being equivalent?
What advantages might a multiple-conclusion sequent have over a one-conclusion sequent?
